{{Short description|Geometric line segment whose endpoints lie on a circular arc}}
{{About|the line segment defined on a curve|other uses|Chord (disambiguation)}}
[[Image:CIRCLE LINES-en.svg|thumb|Common lines and line segments on a circle, including a chord in blue]]

In [[geometry]], a '''chord''' ({{ety|la|chorda|catgut, string}}) of a [[circle]] is a [[straight line segment]] whose endpoints both lie on a [[circular arc]]. If a chord were to be extended [[Infinity|infinitely]] on both directions into a [[Line (geometry)|line]], the object is a ''[[secant line]]''. The perpendicular line passing through the chord's [[midpoint]] is called ''[[Sagitta (geometry)|sagitta]]'' (Latin for "arrow").

More generally, a chord is a line segment joining two points on any [[curve]], for instance, on an [[Ellipse#Chords|ellipse]]. A chord that passes through a circle's center point is the circle's ''[[diameter]]''.

== In circles ==
{{Main|Circle#Chord}}
Among properties of chords of a [[circle]] are the following:
# Chords are equidistant from the center if and only if their lengths are equal.
# Equal chords are subtended by equal angles from the center of the circle.
# A chord that passes through the center of a circle is called a diameter and is the longest chord of that specific circle.
# If the line extensions (secant lines) of chords {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|CD}}}} intersect at a point {{mvar|P}}, then their lengths satisfy {{math|1=''{{overline|AP}}'' · ''{{overline|PB}}'' = ''{{overline|CP}}'' · ''{{overline|PD}}''}} ([[power of a point theorem]]).

==In conics==
The midpoints of a set of parallel chords of a [[conic]] are [[Collinearity|collinear]] ([[ Midpoint theorem (conics)|midpoint theorem for conics]]).<ref>{{cite book |first=C. G.|last=Gibson|year=2003|title=Elementary Euclidean Geometry: An Introduction|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9780521834483|pages=65–68|contribution=7.1 Midpoint Loci|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IdupACBeZEsC&pg=PA65}}</ref>

== <span class="anchor" id="crd"></span><span class="anchor" id="acrd"></span>In trigonometry ==
[[Image:TrigonometricChord.svg|right|200px]]

Chords were used extensively in the early development of [[trigonometry]]. The first known trigonometric table, compiled by [[Hipparchus]] in the 2nd century BC, is no longer extant but [[table of chords|tabulated the value of the chord function]] for every {{frac|7|1|2}} [[Degree (angle)|degree]]s.  In the 2nd century AD, [[Ptolemy]] compiled a more extensive table of chords in [[Almagest|his book on astronomy]], giving the value of the chord for angles ranging from {{frac|1|2}} to 180 degrees by increments of {{frac|1|2}} degree. Ptolemy used a circle of diameter 120, and gave chord lengths accurate to two [[sexagesimal]] (base sixty) digits after the integer part.<ref name=Maor>{{cite book|first=Eli|last=Maor|title=Trigonometric Delights|year=1998|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-15820-4|pages=25–27}}</ref>

The chord function is defined geometrically as shown in the picture. The chord of an [[angle]] is the [[length]] of the chord between two points on a unit circle separated by that [[central angle]]. The angle {{mvar|θ}} is taken in the positive sense and must lie in the interval {{math|0 < ''θ'' ≤ {{pi}}}} (radian measure). The chord function can be related to the modern [[sine]] function, by taking one of the points to be {{math|(1,0)}}, and the other point to be {{math|(cos ''θ'', sin ''θ'')}}, and then using the [[Pythagorean theorem]] to calculate the chord length:<ref name=Maor />

<math display=block> \operatorname{crd} \theta = \sqrt{(1-\cos \theta)^2+\sin^2 \theta} = \sqrt{2-2\cos \theta} =2 \sin \frac{\theta }{2} </math> <ref>Weisstein, Eric W. "[https://mathworld.wolfram.com/CircularSegment.html Circular Segment]". From MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource.</ref>

The last step uses the [[List_of_trigonometric_identities#Half-angle_formulae|half-angle formula]]. Much as modern trigonometry is built on the sine function, ancient trigonometry was built on the chord function. Hipparchus is purported to have written a twelve-volume work on chords, all now lost, so presumably, a great deal was known about them. In the table below (where {{mvar|c}} is the chord length, and {{mvar|D}} the diameter of the circle) the chord function can be shown to satisfy many identities analogous to well-known modern ones:

{| class="wikitable"
!Name!!Sine-based!!Chord-based
|-
|Pythagorean
|<math>\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1 \, </math>
|<math>\operatorname{crd}^2 \theta + \operatorname{crd}^2 (\pi- \theta) = 4 \, </math>
|-
|Half-angle
|<math>\sin\frac{\theta}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos \theta}{2}} \, </math>
|<math>\operatorname{crd}\ \frac{\theta}{2} =  \sqrt{2-\operatorname{crd}(\pi - \theta)} \,</math>
|-
| '''[[Apothem]] ({{mvar|a}})'''
|<math>c=2 \sqrt{r^2- a^2}</math>
|<math>c=\sqrt{D ^2-4 a^2}</math>
|-
| '''Angle ({{mvar|θ}})'''
|<math>c=2 r \sin \frac{\theta }{2}</math>
|<math>c=\frac{D}{2}  \operatorname{crd} \theta</math>
|}

The inverse function exists as well:<ref name="Simpson_2001">{{cite web | title=AUXTRIG | first=David G. | last=Simpson | publisher=NASA Goddard Space Flight Center | location=Greenbelt, Maryland, US | date=2001-11-08 | type=FORTRAN-90 source code |url=http://www.davidgsimpson.com/software/auxtrig_f90.txt | access-date=2015-10-26}}</ref>

<math display="block">\theta = 2\arcsin\frac{c}{2r}</math>
